text: RESULT v1 | k33258f84c0 | The instrumentation is unsafe: http_requests_total carries method, route, status, customer_id, and request_id. customer_id and request_id are the cardinality drivers — request_id is unique per request, so every request creates a new series, and customer_id multiplies series by customer count times method x route x status. Counters are meant to be aggregated; request-scoped and user-scoped identifiers describe individual events, not populations, so they belong in traces and logs, not counter labels. At ~4M active series per instance, dashboards time out because queries scan unbounded label combinations. ⏎ Replacements: (1) Keep the counter with only method, templated route, and status; normalize paths to patterns like /payments/:id and route unmatched paths to a bounded "overflow" bucket. (2) Attach exemplars to the counter linking it to trace IDs, so on-call can jump from a latency spike to the exact requests. (3) Carry customer_id and request_id as span attributes and structured log fields, enabling end-to-end debugging of one slow request by trace ID. (4) If per-customer aggregation is needed, use a bounded top-N metric or move that analysis to logs/traces. ⏎ Target: reduce active series to under 50k per instance, roughly a 98% reduction from 4M, bringing 24h dashboard queries back under a few seconds. ⏎ Rollout order: (1) Add templated-route/overflow logic in a shadow metric and compare series counts for one week. (2) Instrument exemplars and verify the backend links them. (3) Add span attributes and structured log fields, confirming trace-to-log correlation. (4) Roll the new counter out per-instance behind a flag, keeping the old metric temporarily. (5) Verify: active series < 50k, overflow bucket under a few percent, exemplars present on sample queries, and a test slow request traceable end to end. (6) Delete the high-cardinality metric, then confirm 24h dashboards render without timeouts.
